dispositions.sentence: Justin, who told his imperial interrogator that he taught above a public bathhouse in Rome, wrote down the earliest record of what their Sunday actually looked like—the reading of the memoirs, the common loaf and cup, and the collection gathered for orphans, widows, and travelers.

dispositions.sentence: Around 112 CE, the governor Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan describing an investigation: believers who had recanted told him, under threat of ordinary punishment, that these communities met before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ 'as God,' bound themselves by oath against theft and adultery, then met again later for a meal they called 'common yet harmless.'
dispositions.reason: Roman state, no census movement. Supported by the world record pahc.source.pliny-letters (records/pahc/source/) and in part by the Latin of Ep. 10.96 quoted in an editor's note, anf05 60209-60211 ('ante lucem convenire, carmenque Christo, quasi Deo').

dispositions.sentence: In the decades after the apostles died, these house churches held together with no fixed hierarchy and no finished New Testament - Ignatius wrote seven letters while under armed guard on his way to execution, and Rome wrote at length to settle a quarrel in Corinth.

dispositions.sentence: The charges were always roughly the same - that Christians were atheists because they had no images, cannibals because of what they said about eating a body, and disloyal because they would not sacrifice - and the answers were too.

dispositions.sentence: What made the enterprise interesting was the second move: rather than only denying the charges, most of them argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held, and that Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason rather than its enemies.

dispositions.sentence: And at the end of the line stands Lactantius, whom Jerome makes Arnobius' pupil: a professor of Latin rhetoric summoned to Diocletian's new capital at Nicomedia, who lost the post when the persecution began and wrote the Divine Institutes in the middle of it ...

prose_changes.old: Parent of nearly everything on the map
prose_changes.new: The earliest layer on the map, which most later traditions claim as their root

prose_changes.old: Almost every Christian tradition descends from these early gatherings.
prose_changes.new: Almost every Christian tradition claims a root in these early gatherings.
prose_changes.reason: Same reason: descent is stated as fact with no line to most traditions documented; what is true is that they claim it.

prose_changes.old: Overlaps post-apostolic-house-church in era and largely in people - Justin taught at Rome - but is a different thing: that entry is the church's internal life, this is the same Christians turned outward, addressing emperors and an educated public that despised them.
prose_changes.new: It overlaps the household churches of the same years, in time and in people. Justin taught at Rome, Theophilus was bishop of Antioch and Melito bishop of Sardis. But it is a different thing. The household churches show the church's inner life. Here the church turns outward, to emperors and an educated public that despised it.
prose_changes.reason: Removes a census ID and 'that entry' from public text. 'Largely in people' and 'the same Christians' rested on Justin alone; now names the documented overlap: Justin's own Sunday 'we' (1 Apol. 67, anf01 16502-16528), Theophilus 'sixth from the apostles' in the church of Antioch (Eusebius HE IV.20, npnf201 24429-24430), Melito 'bishop of the parish in Sardis' (HE IV.26, npnf201 25471-25472).

prose_changes.old: What made the enterprise interesting was the second move: rather than only denying the charges, most of them argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held, and that Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason rather than its enemies.
prose_changes.new: What made the enterprise interesting was the second move. Several of them, Justin above all, did more than deny the charges. They argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held. Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason, not its enemies.
prose_changes.reason: 'Most of them' overstates: Justin (2 Apol. 8, 13: 'seed of reason', 'spermatic word', anf01 17036, 17231-17236) and Athenagoras make the case, but Diognetus 8 scorns 'the empty and silly doctrines' of philosophers (anf01 2868) and Theophilus and Tatian are largely hostile. Also splits a 47-word sentence.

prose_changes.old: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down, and that Clement and Origen at Alexandria took much further.
prose_changes.new: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down. Clement at Alexandria spoke the same way of philosophers receiving 'the seeds of the Truth', and he and Origen took the approach much further.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored Alexandrian text names Justin for this idea (2026-11-06 wanted-texts list), so the sentence no longer says they took Justin's argument further. It states the documented parallel: Clement, Strom. VI.7, 'if from any creature they received in any way whatever the seeds of the Truth' (anf02 46779-46780). The movement-level link stays the existing Tatian one.
